title: The Little Ice Age

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The Little Ice Age was a period of unusually cold conditions between approximately AD 1300 and 1850 which affected the northern hemisphere. However, there was no single, well-defined period of prolonged extreme cold; instead there were two clearly defined phases, with the first beginning around 1290 and continuing until the late 1400s. There was a slightly warmer period in the 1500s, after which the climate deteriorated substantially, with the coldest period, known as the Maunder Minimum, between 1645 and 1715. During this phase of the Little Ice Age, there are indications that average winter temperatures were as much as 2°C lower than at present.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: During the Little Ice Age, winters were bitterly cold and prolonged and summers were often cool and wet, reducing the growing season by several weeks. These conditions often led to widespread crop failure and a huge increase in grain prices. As a result, there was greater social instability as large parts of the population were reduced to poverty and even starvation. Some historians have argued that the fall of the ruling Ming dynasty in China may have been partially caused by a succession of poor harvests. Frequent shortages of basic supplies led to malnutrition, which meant people were also less able to resist disease. Consequently, there were notable decreases in population in parts of France and central Europe during the mid to late seventeenth century. Much of Scandinavia suffered particularly badly, with Finland possibly losing up to a third of its population.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There were even times when the Baltic Sea froze over. Pack ice expanded far south into the Atlantic, preventing ships from travelling to ports in Iceland for months on end. Fishing in northern Europe was also badly affected, as cod migrated south to find warmer water. Tax records in Scandinavia show many villages and farms in rural areas were destroyed by the advance of glaciers. In mountainous regions such as the Alps, the same pattern was observable, with the glaciers threatening to overwhelm entire towns. Then during brief warmer periods when the ice in lakes and rivers melted, severe flooding posed a serious threat to human life and property.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Some countries rose to the challenges posed by the increasingly severe climatic conditions far better than others. In England and the Netherlands, agricultural methods were revolutionised in order to deal with the shortened, less reliable growing season. Agriculture was also diversified, with a wide range of new crops being planted, many of which could withstand lower temperatures. These countries also had the advantage of good trade links, so they could easily increase imports of staples such as grain when harvests failed. Increased trade also gave a few of them the financial resources to develop technological solutions, such as innovations in shipbuilding and engineering.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The exact cause of this long period of low temperatures is unknown. However, scientists have observed a striking correlation between the timing of the Little Ice Age and the number of sunspots* on the surface of the sun. During this period, there were notably fewer sunspots, indicating a less active sun. This was most obvious between 1460 and 1550 and again during the Maunder Minimum between 1645 and 1715. It is thought likely that much less radiation than average was emitted by the sun during the Maunder Minimum, and research by climatologists suggests this may have reduced average global temperatures by 0.4°C. However, even this does not entirely account for the Little Ice Age.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One other theory is that throughout the Little Ice Age, the world experienced heightened volcanic activity. When volcanoes erupt, the ash produced forms vast clouds reaching high into the atmosphere and even spreading to cover the whole earth. These block out the sun, leading to a worldwide cooling. A recent study found that a massive eruption occurred in 1257 in Indonesia, followed by three smaller ones in 1268, 1275 and 1284, and there is speculation that this may have caused the initial cooling. The 1452-53 eruption in Vanuatu in the South Pacific may have triggered a second period of falling temperatures.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Other scientists focus on the oceans, particularly the North Atlantic, which is one of the most climatically unstable regions in the world. One feature of this instability is a phenomenon known as the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO), which is defined as the constantly fluctuating differences between the atmospheric pressure over Iceland and over the islands of the Azores. When the generally high pressure over the Azores grows stronger than usual and the Icelandic low becomes deeper than normal, the result in northern Europe is winters that are unsettled but basically mild. This indicates what is called a positive NAO index. However, when both pressure systems are weak, cold air can reach northern Europe more easily during the winter months which results In very cold conditions. Storms are also much more frequent than usual, especially in the Mediterranean. These conditions correspond to a negative NAO index. Many climatologists now believe that during the Little Ice Age, the NAO index was more consistently negative compared to earlier and later periods.

groups.title: Causes of the Little Ice Age
content: Scientists have noted that the periods of most severe weather coincided with a significant lack of sunspots, a phenomenon associated with a fall in the amount of {{23}} produced by the sun. Other scientists highlight the fact that several {{24}} were particularly active during certain periods of the Little Ice Age. At these times, sunlight was prevented from reaching the earth’s surface by an enormous amount of ash in the atmosphere.

Another theory focuses on variation in the {{25}} above two parts of the Atlantic Ocean. If the difference between the two is comparatively small, then the winter in the northern hemisphere is very cold and the Mediterranean is more likely to experience {{26}}. It is thought that during the Little Ice Age, this weather pattern occurred more often than before.
